ideas.concern: The voice call to an airline is staged with a teammate, so real-world robustness is unproven. The team also needs to compute DOT refund eligibility correctly (what counts as a significant change) rather than hand-wave it.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: The pain is real but annual and slow-moving. The multi-year dormancy part runs on synthetic data, so the demo lacks a live 'money recovered' moment, and multi-state NAUPA compliance is easy to get subtly wrong.

verdict.why_winner: C takes A's recovery-agent concept and gives it a concrete, legally grounded wedge. The DOT 14 CFR 260 cash-refund rule turns a vague 'find disputes' tool into a quantifiable recovery engine against a material slice of corporate air spend. The escalation path (inbox matching, then refund request, then voice call, then dispute with transcript as evidence) fills a gap Ramp doesn't automate. It demos credibly end-to-end with the Ramp sandbox and Stripe Issuing test disputes, and it still covers SaaS renewals and duplicate charges. A is the weakest: it is a less focused subset of C with self-admitted thin pain.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: This is the unfocused version of Idea C. The pitch itself concedes disputes are rare and dollar amounts modest, so the 'why would a finance team care' story is thin, and without a concrete merchant scenario the voice-call and evidence-gathering pieces will look generic and scripted in a 3-minute demo. Ramp already surfaces the duplicates; the only new part is the dispute packet, which is a form filler.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: The pain is real and Ramp genuinely has nothing here, but the interesting half (dormancy tracking, due-diligence letters, NAUPA files for 3 states) runs entirely on synthetic multi-year data, and the demo-able half (email a vendor, verify ACH, reissue) is a fairly standard outreach workflow. Hard to make exciting in 3-5 minutes, and ACH fraud verification will likely be hand-waved.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Scope creep is the risk: email-to-transaction matching, rule interpretation, voice calls, Stripe disputes and SaaS renewals is a lot for 10 days, and the SaaS/duplicate tail should be cut. The airline voice call with a teammate will be rehearsed, so I'd want to see it handle an off-script refusal. Also ensure the refund-owed logic is actually derived from the itinerary, not hardcoded.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: Ramp for Construction already validates waivers and Siteline/Procore Pay already generate and chase them, so the differentiated piece shrinks to e-sign dispatch plus a statutory text diff, which is a regex/LLM comparison rather than a hard technical problem. Judges will need a primer on conditional vs unconditional waivers, eating demo time, and the payment-gating hook into Ramp can't be shown for real.

verdict.why_winner: C is the only pitch with a specific regulation (14 CFR 260) that creates a clear, quantifiable pot of money (5-10% of corporate air spend) that Ramp flags but does not recover, a tight end-to-end story that fits in 3-5 minutes, and a demo that can be shown live with the Ramp sandbox, Stripe Issuing test disputes and a live voice call. It does not duplicate what Ramp ships, the admin-approval gate is the right product instinct, and the escalation ladder (ask nicely, call, then dispute with transcript as evidence) is a credible agent workflow a team of three can actually finish in 10 days.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: The pain is real but niche and annual, and the most interesting part (dormancy tracking, due-diligence letters, NAUPA reports) runs on synthetic multi-year data. The live demo will mostly show an outreach email plus a generated report, which may feel thin and hard to make dramatic in 3-5 minutes.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: It heavily overlaps with Ramp for Construction's existing waiver check and with Siteline/Procore Pay. The novel pieces (collection, statutory diffing, gating the unconditional waiver on payment) are incremental, and the construction primer eats demo time.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: The dispute volume and dollars per company are modest, so the ROI story is weak. Without a concrete wedge it reads as a generic 'dispute bot', and reason-code mapping in Stripe test mode can look superficial.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: Scope is broad: airfare rules, voice calls, disputes, plus SaaS and duplicates. Correctly computing what's owed under 14 CFR 260 (what counts as a significant change, partial-use itineraries) is tricky, and a staged teammate-as-airline call risks looking scripted.

verdict.why_winner: D takes C's recovery-agent concept and gives it a sharp, legally grounded wedge. The DOT refund rule creates a concrete entitlement, and travel credits stranded in personal loyalty accounts are a believable, sizable leak of corporate spend that Ramp doesn't automate. The escalation ladder (inbox match, rule-based entitlement, request, live voice call, then a dispute with the transcript as evidence) shows off current AI tools across several modalities. It makes a clear 3-5 minute demo on the Ramp sandbox and Stripe test mode with a visible dollar outcome. B is my least favorite because its core validation already ships in Ramp and competitors cover the rest.

ideas.label: A
ideas.concern: Scope creep: inbox matching, DOT-rule reasoning, a live voice agent, and dispute filing is a lot for 10 days; the SaaS-renewal and duplicate add-ons should be cut so the airfare path is bulletproof. The teammate-as-airline-agent call must be unscripted enough to feel real, and the refund math must handle partial credits correctly or judges will poke holes.

ideas.label: B
ideas.concern: Ramp for Construction already validates waivers and Siteline/Procore already chase them, so the novel slice is narrow (collection + statutory diff). Judges will spend the first minute learning what a lien waiver is, and the end-to-end flow depends on e-signature and payment-clear webhooks that are easy to fake and hard to make feel live.

ideas.label: C
ideas.concern: Genuinely untouched by Ramp and clever, but the pain is annual, low-salience, and modest in dollars for most Ramp customers. Half the demo (dormancy tracking, NAUPA reports) runs on synthetic multi-year data, which judges will see as a mocked spreadsheet rather than an agent doing work; the vendor outreach and ACH-fraud check is the only part that demos live.

ideas.label: D
ideas.concern: This is Idea A without the wedge: no regulatory hook that makes the agent's claim defensible, self-admitted rare disputes and modest dollars, and it overlaps most with what Ramp already ships (duplicate flagging). A generic 'find disputable charges' agent is hard to demo credibly because every case is a different merchant and reason code.

verdict.why_winner: A takes a workflow Ramp explicitly leaves manual (recovery, not just flagging), anchors it to a concrete federal rule that gives the agent a legally grounded ask, and sizes the pain in a category Ramp already sells (travel). The demo is the most credible of the four: sandbox transactions, a real inbox match, a live voice negotiation, then an escalation to a Stripe-issued dispute with transcript evidence and a human approval gate. It shows judgment, tool use, and a clear money-recovered number on screen, which is exactly what the prompt and rubric reward. D is the weakest because it is the same idea diluted, with the most overlap with existing Ramp features and the least demoable specificity.
